chunks.arabic_text: وَبِهَذَا الْإِسْنَادِ عَنْ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ أَحْمَدَ عَنْ مُعَاوِيَةَ بْنِ عَمَّارٍ قَالَ

translations.en: And with this chain of narration, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said:

chunks.arabic_text: قَالَ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ع إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَمْ يُؤْمِنِ الْمُؤْمِنَ مِنْ بَلَايَا الدُّنْيَا وَلَكِنْ آمَنَهُ مِنَ الْعَمَى فِي الْآخِرَةِ وَمِنَ الشَّقَاءِ يَعْنِي عَمَى الْبَصَرِ

translations.en: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: Allah has not guaranteed the believer against the misfortunes of the world, but He has guaranteed him against blindness in the Hereafter and from unhappiness – meaning blindness of the sight.

en.summary: In Sifat al-Shia, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that divine protection for the believer is eschatological rather than temporal, ensuring deliverance from the 'blindness of the heart' that leads to eternal wretchedness. This distinction highlights the Shia understanding that worldly trials (balāyā) serve as purification, while the true guarantee of faith is preservation from spiritual ignorance (ʿamāʾ) in the Hereafter. The hadith thus reorients the believer’s focus from avoiding suffering to securing ultimate salvation through spiritual insight.
en.seo_question: What is the difference between worldly trials and Hereafter's blindness for believers according to Imam al-Sadiq?
